title: COP17: Which countries have released new pledges to tackle nature loss? - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon Brief finds 113 of 196 parties (58%) have submitted new national biodiversity strategies and action plans (NBSAPs), up from 55 a year earlier, two years after the original COP16 deadline. Megadiverse holdouts include Papua New Guinea, Peru, South Africa and the US, as COP17 in Yerevan begins the first global review of the Kunming-Montreal framework.

insights.claim: 113 of 196 parties (58%) have now submitted new national biodiversity strategies and action plans (NBSAPs), up from 55 countries a year earlier, per Carbon Brief analysis.
insights.speaker: Daisy Dunne
insights.so_what: Benchmark for how far national nature-policy follow-through lags UN deadlines; track the count at and after COP17.

insights.claim: Only 15% of nations met the original deadline to file NBSAPs by the start of COP16 in October 2024, and the COP16 text only 'urges' countries to file 'as soon as possible', so the deadline carries no hard enforcement.
insights.speaker: Daisy Dunne
insights.so_what: Soft-urging language implies weak compliance pressure; expect further slippage on COP17-era commitments.

insights.claim: Many African nations (including Egypt, Ethiopia, DRC, Zambia, Zimbabwe) and South American nations (including Brazil, Belize, Chile) published new NBSAPs over the past year, and host nation Armenia published in April.
insights.speaker: Daisy Dunne
insights.so_what: Biodiverse emerging markets are formalising nature plans, a precondition for accessing nature finance.
insights.locator: Since last year, many African nations...

insights.claim: Four megadiverse nations holding most of Earth's species (Papua New Guinea, Peru, South Africa and the US) and Russia, the country with the most land, have not published new NBSAPs.
insights.speaker: Daisy Dunne
insights.so_what: Key biodiversity and resource jurisdictions are outside the plan process, a risk to the credibility of the global review.
insights.locator: Four of the world's megadiverse nations...

insights.claim: The US is the only UN member country that is not a signatory to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity.
insights.speaker: Daisy Dunne
insights.so_what: US absence limits leverage over US-based corporate and finance actors in nature policy.
insights.locator: Four of the world's megadiverse nations...

insights.claim: COP17 in Yerevan, Armenia is the halfway point of the 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (23 targets for 2030) and hosts the first global review of country progress, informed by a UN global report drawing on NBSAPs, national targets and seventh national reports.
insights.speaker: Daisy Dunne
insights.so_what: The review is the catalyst for headlines on target shortfalls and negotiation over finance and accountability.

insights.claim: Countries with at least one national target rose from 119 at the end of COP16 to 175 (89%), and seventh national reports submitted rose from about half to 73%, so reporting is improving faster than full plans.
insights.speaker: Daisy Dunne
insights.so_what: Reporting coverage is improving, which strengthens the data behind the global review, though targets without plans do not show how goals will be achieved.
insights.locator: By the end of COP16, some 119 parties...

insights.claim: Developing countries say lack of funding has prevented them from publishing NBSAPs, while the Global Environment Facility says 120 of 139 countries that requested support since COP16 accessed it and the remaining 19 are awaiting resolution of outstanding issues via UNEP.
insights.speaker: Daisy Dunne
insights.so_what: Finance access, not only political will, gates national nature planning; watch the unresolved 19 countries.
